name: moon_shadow_twilight_fade
description: §6b: the moon shadow fades in during nautical twilight rather than popping on at sunset. Walks lat 45 / day 37 (full moon) from just before sunset to deep night and pins where the shadow is absent, where it has arrived, and where it has saturated. The moon_shadow_render expectations track the SHIPPED PRESET's shadow-strength slider (CelestialSettingsMath.Presets.Cinematic.ShadowStrength, currently 0.8). Recompute after a preset change: rendered = 1 - MoonShadowStrength(illum, moonElev, sunElev) * ShadowStrength * (1 - 0.107), where 0.107 is MoonMath.MoonShadowColorValue(0.25, 0.28).
_comment: Same tile as moon_sun_clock.json (lat 45, day 37, moon exactly full at noon) so the two read
against one another: that scenario proves the moon rides the warped clock, this one proves the
shadow it casts arrives at the right BRIGHTNESS rather than at the right moon position.
Before §6b the moon shadow switched on the instant the sun passed the refraction horizon, at
whatever strength the moon's altitude implied — 0.881 at hour 21.3 here, in a sky still ~9 lux
against the full moon's 0.27. This scenario's hour-21.3 probe is that regression, inverted: it
must now read a clean 1.0 (no shadow at all).
The sun_elevation probes are the anchors, and they are exact — they come from the same
SunClockMath warp the mod runs, calibrated against this scenario family's own live-probed 7.39
at hour 20. They fix which twilight phase each moment is in, so a moon_shadow_render reading
cannot be explained away as 'the clock moved' when what changed was the shadow model.
Deliberately NOT probed: the steep middle of the fade (hours 21.6-21.8, where the render sweeps
0.96 -> 0.83). Contrast there is changing fast enough that pinning it would be pinning the
sub-degree accuracy of the moon's position rather than the fade, and the timelapse below already
shows that stretch to a human. The three pinned points bracket it: nothing at 21.3, arrived by

steps._comment: Guard against a vacuous run: if this is not a full moon, every expectation below is meaningless.

Hour 21.0 — two minutes BEFORE vanilla's sunset (21.032), sun still 0.58 deg up. The SUN still owns the shadow here, so this reads the sun branch's near-zero-elevation value. Probed to fix which side of the caster handover we start on; §6b must not move it.

THE REGRESSION PROBE. Hour 21.3, sun 4.8 deg below the horizon — past the caster handover, so the sun's shadow is gone, and the old model started the moon's here at 0.881. The sky is still ~8.9 lux, ~33x the full moon, so §6b says there is nothing to see. A failure here reading ~0.88 means the sun-below-horizon gate is back.

Hour 21.5, end of civil twilight (sun -7.6, sky ~0.66 lux). Still nothing: a full moon needs the sky about 2x darker again before it can register. This is the probe that pins the fade as LATE rather than merely soft — a model that started the shadow at sunset but ramped it slowly would pass 21.3 and fail here.

Hour 22.0, mid nautical twilight (sun -14.2, sky ~0.004 lux). The moon now dominates and the shadow has essentially arrived. Tolerance is wider than the endpoints because this sits on the shoulder of the curve, where a degree of moon altitude is still worth ~0.005 of render.
Hour 23.0, full darkness (sun -24, sky at the starlight floor). Saturated: the ratio is ~0.997 and the render sits on the artistic cap. Flat enough here that a tight tolerance is safe.
Off/on A/B at the saturated end, so the deep-night shadow is shown to be OURS and not something vanilla was drawing anyway.

The fade itself, for a human: one frame every 0.05 h from just before sunset to full darkness. This is where the steep middle the probes skip actually gets reviewed — what it must NOT show is a single-frame step from no shadow to full shadow.
Leave the clock somewhere harmless for whatever runs next.
